title: The Man in Two Gloves: Aaron Rai Makes History as First Indian-Heritage Golfer to Win a Major
excerpt: The 31-year-old Wolverhampton native closed with a five-under 65 at Aronimink to capture the PGA Championship, becoming the first Englishman to lift the Wanamaker Trophy in 107 years
body:
When Aaron Rai sank a 68-foot eagle on the 17th hole at Aronimink Golf Club on Sunday, he didn't just win a golf tournament. He wrote himself into history — twice over.

The 31-year-old from Wolverhampton, England, closed with a scintillating five-under-par 65 to capture the 108th PGA Championship at nine under par, beating Jon Rahm and Alex Smalley by three strokes. In doing so, he became the first Englishman to lift the Wanamaker Trophy since Jim Barnes in 1919 — and the first golfer of Indian heritage ever to win a men's major championship.

## From Wolverhampton to Wanamaker

Rai's path to the winner's circle at Aronimink reads like no other story in professional golf. Born to a family of Indian-Kenyan descent in the West Midlands, he grew up swinging clubs at a municipal course, his father Baldev Rai encouraging a young Aaron's grip by handing him a second glove — a habit that has become the golfer's trademark two-glove setup, still visible on golf's biggest stage.

He turned professional at 17, too early by his own admission. "I wasn't ready," he once told Golf Digest. Years of grinding on the Challenge Tour and the DP World Tour followed, with a breakthrough Scottish Open win in 2020 and, finally, a PGA Tour card. His first Tour victory came at the 2024 Wyndham Championship. Sunday's triumph was something else entirely.

## A Final Round for the Ages

Rai entered the final round two shots behind the leaders, with Rory McIlroy, Scottie Scheffler, and Jon Rahm all within striking distance. What followed was controlled chaos. Rai birdied the fourth and fifth holes, then dropped a 40-foot eagle putt on the ninth to take the lead. When he appeared to wobble with a bogey on 14, the leaderboard compressed. Four players were within one stroke.

Then came the 17th — a moment that will be replayed for decades. From 68 feet, on a slick, undulating green, Rai's eagle putt tracked the ridge, curled right, and dropped. He pumped his fist — a rare display of emotion from one of golf's most measured competitors — and the roar at Aronimink told the story. The three-shot margin at the finish line barely captured how tight the afternoon had been.

## The Bishnoi Factor

Waiting behind the 18th green was Gaurika Bishnoi, Rai's wife and herself a professional golfer. Born in India and a product of the Hero Women's Pro Golf Tour — where she has eight career victories — Bishnoi has been a constant presence in Rai's corner. The couple married in July 2025, and she famously stole the show at the 2025 Masters Par-3 Contest with a shot that drew praise from Max Homa.

Their embrace after the final putt carried the weight of two careers, two cultures, and one shared dream. "She understands the game better than anyone around me," Rai said.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

Aaron Rai joins Vijay Singh — the Fijian-Indian great who won three majors — as a golfer of South Asian descent to capture one of golf's biggest prizes. But where Singh's heritage was acknowledged quietly, Rai's victory arrives in a different era, one where representation in elite sport is celebrated loudly.

Three golfers of Indian origin — Rai, Sahith Theegala, and Akshay Bhatia — now compete regularly on the PGA Tour, a transformation unthinkable a decade ago. For the estimated 4.4 million Indian-Americans and millions more in the global diaspora, Rai's win is proof that the country-club sport is no longer someone else's game.

In desi households from Birmingham to the Bay Area, Sunday's conversation wasn't about cricket. It was about golf — and a quiet man in two gloves who made history at nine under par.

## What's Next

Rai pockets $3.6 million from the $20.5 million purse and secures exemptions into future majors through 2031. He is expected to be a strong candidate for the 2027 European Ryder Cup team. For British Asians and the global Indian diaspora, the question now is simpler: what ceiling?
